Give me a design checklist for a production webhook handler - the things that must be true before we point a provider at it. We have been bitten by duplicates, slow handlers, and signature problems, and I want the review criteria in one place.

A production webhook handler has to survive the provider's contract, which is: at-least-once delivery, no ordering guarantee, retries for hours to days, and payloads that evolve. Review against this list:

| Concern | Requirement | Failure it prevents |
|---|---|---|
| Signature | Verify against the raw request body, before parsing | Reserialization mismatches; forged events |
| Ack speed | Persist the raw event, return 200 in well under the provider's timeout; process asynchronously | Timeout retries duplicating side effects |
| Idempotency | Dedupe on the provider's event id, stored with a uniqueness constraint | Double billing on redelivery |
| Dedupe lifetime | Retention longer than the provider's full retry window | Late redeliveries reprocessed after expiry |
| Ordering | Never assume arrival order; order by event created time or re-fetch object state | Stale state overwriting fresh state |
| Unknown types | Log and dead-letter unrecognized event types, never silently drop | Provider renames silently eating events |
| Failure split | 5xx only for transient faults; store poison events and ack them | Retry storms on permanently failing payloads |
| Observability | Per-type delivery counts, ack latency, dedupe hit rate on a dashboard | 'Webhooks stopped working' as a surprise |
| Secrets | One secret per endpoint; support old + new during rotation | Rotation day breaking every verification |
| Replay | A way to reprocess stored raw events after a handler fix | Events lost to a since-fixed bug |

The unifying principle: the endpoint itself should be tiny - verify, store, ack - and everything interesting should happen in workers that can be slow, retried, and replayed without the provider's clock ticking.

Checkout double-submits - a double-click, a browser retry, a user refreshing a slow page - create two charges for one purchase on an API that supports idempotency keys, because our client sends none. Simulate the endpoint with and without a key:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
no key, double submit:   ['created ch_1', 'created ch_2'] | charges: 2
with key, double submit: ['created ch_1', 'replayed ch_1'] | charges: 1

Without a key, the server cannot tell a double-submit from two purchases - the two requests are identical strangers, so it creates ch_1 and ch_2 and the customer pays twice. With an idempotency key, the second request is recognized as the same operation and the server replays the original result ('replayed ch_1') without executing anything: one charge, and both callers get a consistent answer. That is the whole mechanism - the key is a name the client gives the operation, so the server can collapse every retry of that operation into its first execution. The client-side obligations are what make or break it: the key must be generated once per logical operation (per checkout, per payment intent), stored with the operation, and reused by every retry, refresh, and resubmission of that same operation - and a genuinely new purchase must get a fresh key, or it will be swallowed as a replay of the old one. Generate the key when the user starts the checkout, not when the request is sent. Every layer that can retry - browser, load balancer, your own retry loop - becomes safe the moment the key is stable.

Our client DOES send idempotency keys - I verified they are in the headers - yet a retried payment still double-charged. The retry logic generates the key inside the request function: every attempt calls uuid4() and sends 'Idempotency-Key: <fresh uuid>'. The purchase was attempted 3 times (two timeouts, then success). Model what the server saw:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
attempt results: ['created ch_1', 'created ch_2', 'created ch_3']
charges created for one purchase: 3

The keys are present and useless: three attempts carried three different keys, so the server saw three unrelated operations and created three charges. An idempotency key identifies the operation, not the attempt - generating it inside the request function guarantees it changes exactly when it must not, on every retry. It is the distributed-systems version of introducing yourself with a new name each time you repeat a question and wondering why nobody says 'you already asked that'. The fix is about where the key is born: generate it at the moment the logical operation is created (the checkout session, the payment intent, the order draft), persist it alongside that operation's record, and have every attempt - retry, timeout recovery, page refresh, even a second device resuming the checkout - read the same stored key. Only a new operation mints a new key. A quick audit finds this bug anywhere: log the key alongside the operation id and count distinct keys per operation; the healthy number is exactly 1, and anything above it means your retries are reintroducing themselves as strangers.

A client's integration sends the literal string 'idem-1' as the Idempotency-Key on every request - the developer copied a docs example. First purchase works. Second purchase, a different item at a different price, fails with a 422 the client logs as a server malfunction. Simulate the server's view:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
201: created
200: replayed original result
422: idempotency key already used with a different payload

The server is doing exactly what idempotency requires, and the 422 is it refusing to let one key name two different operations. A key promises 'the request with this key is always the same operation'. When 'idem-1' arrives with the book payload twice, the server replays the original result - correct. When the same key arrives with a laptop payload, the server cannot both honor the promise and execute the request, so it rejects with 422: the key has been spent on a different operation. From the server's chair, a reused key with a changed payload is either a client bug or an attack, and neither deserves execution. The client's actual bugs are two: minting the key once (from a documentation example, no less) instead of once per operation, and logging a 422 - a client-correctable rejection whose body explains itself - as a server malfunction. The rule to internalize: key equality is a claim of operation equality. If two requests differ in anything that matters, they must carry different keys; if they are the same operation retried, they must carry the same key and byte-identical payloads.

Our team is confused about idempotency key scope. We use the same key format everywhere, and two questions keep coming up: (1) if we reuse a key from POST /charges on POST /refunds, does it dedupe across endpoints? (2) our staging and production environments share a key-generation service - is a key spent in staging also spent in production? Settle both, and give us the general rule.

Neither dedupes, and the general rule is that an idempotency key lives inside a namespace with three walls: the account, the endpoint (operation type), and the environment. (1) Across endpoints: no. A key on POST /charges names a charge operation; the same string on POST /refunds names a refund operation, and servers key their idempotency store by (account, endpoint, key) precisely so that operations of different kinds cannot collide. Reusing the string is harmless but meaningless - it buys no protection on the second endpoint, where the refund still needs its own key discipline. (2) Across environments: also no, and this one matters more. Staging and production are separate systems with separate stores; a key consumed in staging has no existence in production. The trap hiding in your setup is the opposite direction: because the generator is shared, make sure it cannot mint the same key twice for two different real operations (a UUID generator is fine; a counter that resets per environment is not, if the values ever cross over through copied data or a merged config). Practical guidance: treat the dedupe space as (environment, account, endpoint, key); generate keys as UUIDs at operation creation; never design a workflow that depends on a key meaning anything outside the one endpoint and environment where the operation lives.

An idempotency mystery: a payment was executed twice from ONE key, three days apart, and the provider's support confirms both executions used key 'idem-x'. The provider retains idempotency keys for 24 hours. The attempts: hour 0 original, hour 2 a retry, hour 30 a retry of the same operation after a long outage on our side. Walk the retention:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
hour 0 original -> EXECUTED (key not retained)
hour 2 retry -> replayed, no execution
hour 30 retry after outage -> EXECUTED (key not retained)

The key did not fail - it expired. At hour 2 the retry found the key retained and replayed harmlessly. At hour 30, the key's 24-hour retention had lapsed, so the provider treated the request as a first sighting and executed it: a second real charge from a correctly-formed retry. Idempotency is a lease, not a law of nature - the dedupe guarantee lasts exactly as long as the provider stores the key, and retention windows (commonly 24 hours) are documented contract terms, not implementation details. This shapes retry design on your side: retries are safe inside the window, so a client should complete its retry story well within it; a retry that wakes up after the window - a queue drained a day later, a dead-letter replayed next week - must not blindly resend the original request. The safe pattern for late recovery is reconcile-first: query the provider for the operation's outcome by your own reference, and only create if the original truly never landed. Operationally, treat 'retry after >24h' as a different species from 'retry': it is a new decision, made with fresh evidence, not the tail of an old loop.

A legacy reporting endpoint is defined as GET /invoices/generate?customer=123 and - despite being a GET - it creates a new invoice on every call. Invoices are duplicating. The access logs show the extra calls come from a corporate proxy retrying the request, a browser prefetch, and our own monitoring tool. The team asks why a GET is being called repeatedly at all, and whose bug the duplicates are.

The duplicates are the endpoint's bug, and the repeated calls are the internet working as specified. GET is defined as a safe method: it must not change state, and precisely because of that promise, every intermediary between client and server is licensed to repeat it freely - proxies retry it, browsers prefetch it, crawlers follow it, monitors poll it, and users refresh it, all without asking anyone. An endpoint that creates an invoice on GET has opted out of that protection while keeping the label, so it gets duplicated by infrastructure that is behaving correctly. No amount of asking the proxy team to stop will fix this; there will always be another prefetcher. The repair is on the endpoint: move invoice creation to POST (the method whose semantics say 'this changes state'), protect that POST with an idempotency key so even POST-level retries collapse, and leave GET /invoices/{id} for retrieval, which can then be cached and retried harmlessly. Audit for siblings while you are at it: any GET with a verb in its path - generate, send, process, delete - is the same bug wearing a different name, and each one is duplicating something quietly.

The scariest idempotency case: a charge POST executes on the server, but the response is lost to a network timeout, so the client cannot tell whether it was charged. Walk what happens with and without an idempotency key when the client retries - server state is the only truth here:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
attempt 1 (keyed, response lost): client sees: TIMEOUT (charge already exists)
attempt 2 (same key):             replayed ch_1
charges on server: 1

This is the scenario idempotency keys exist for, and the walk shows the key converting an unknowable situation into a safe retry. Attempt 1 executed - ch_1 exists - but the response vanished into a timeout, leaving the client in the worst state in distributed systems: the operation may or may not have happened. Without a key, any choice is a gamble: retry and risk a double charge, or don't and risk a lost sale. With the key, attempt 2 is not a new execution at all - the server finds 'idem-55' in its store and replays the original outcome, so the client learns the truth ('replayed ch_1') while the charge count stays at exactly 1. Note what the key really bought: not prevention of the retry, but safety in making it. The design corollaries: the server must store the key with the completed result (including failures it intends to be final) for the retention window, and the client must treat a timeout on a keyed request as 'retry to learn the outcome', never as 'failed'. Timeouts are ambiguous; keys are how you afford to resolve the ambiguity.

A loyalty-points API offers PATCH /members/7 with {"points_delta": +50}. A client's request succeeded but the response was lost, the client retried the identical PATCH, and the member ended up with 200 points instead of the intended 150 (starting from 100). Reproduce, then state the fix:

arguments.code:
points = 100
def patch_delta(d):
    global points
    points += d
    return points
print("after first PATCH +50: ", patch_delta(50))
print("after retried PATCH +50:", patch_delta(50))
print("intended balance: 150 | actual balance:", points)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
after first PATCH +50:  150
after retried PATCH +50: 200
intended balance: 150 | actual balance: 200

The retry applied the increment twice because a delta is an instruction to change state, not a description of the desired state - and instructions re-executed are effects re-applied. The first PATCH moved 100 to 150 and its response was lost; the identical retry moved 150 to 200. Nothing malfunctioned: the server executed two valid requests. Contrast with a state-describing request - PATCH {"points": 150} - which can be retried any number of times and converges to 150, because applying a description twice is the same as applying it once. That property, natural idempotency, is why mature APIs prefer absolute updates, PUT-style replacements, and 'set' semantics over deltas and increments for anything a client might retry. Where deltas are unavoidable (counters, append operations), the operation needs an idempotency key or a client-supplied operation id the server records, so the second arrival is recognized as the same instruction. The general lesson: before adding retry logic anywhere, ask of each request 'what happens if this executes twice?' If the answer is not 'the same as once', the retry is a bug generator, and the fix belongs to the request's shape or its keying, not to the retry count.

A subscription service derives each request's idempotency key by hashing the request payload. Monday, a customer buys a plan (payload: customer cus_4, amount 2500) and is charged. Tuesday, the same customer deliberately buys the same plan again as a gift - identical payload - and is NOT charged, yet receives a success response. Reproduce the key collision:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
monday purchase: created ch_1
tuesday purchase: replayed ch_1 - success response, NO new charge
charges created: 1

Content-derived keys cannot distinguish 'the same operation retried' from 'the same purchase made again', and Tuesday's gift fell into that blind spot. Because the key is a hash of the payload, two operations with identical payloads get identical keys by construction, so the server faithfully replayed Monday's result and created nothing - the customer got a success response for a charge that never happened, arguably worse than a double charge because no money trail exists to audit. An idempotency key must identify the operation instance, which is a fact about the client's intent, not about the request bytes: it should be a fresh random value (UUID) minted when the operation is created and stored with it. Identical twins are the test that separates the two designs - retries of one operation share an intent and must share a key; two operations share only content and must not. This is the request-side twin of deduping webhooks by payload hash: in both directions, identity comes from an id assigned to the event or operation, never from hashing what it contains. Content hashes are for integrity checking; ids are for identity. Confusing the two manufactures exactly-once violations in both directions.

We are adding idempotency support to our payments API and client. Give me the design decisions as a table: where keys come from, what they are scoped to, how long they live, what gets stored, and what happens on conflicts - with the reasoning, not just the choices.

Idempotency is a small protocol with five load-bearing decisions:

| Decision | Sound choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Key origin | Client generates a UUID when the logical operation is created (checkout, order draft), stores it with the operation | Only the client knows which attempts belong to the same operation |
| Key form | Random and opaque - never derived from the payload | Identical repeat purchases must get different keys; retries must reuse the same one |
| Scope | (environment, account, endpoint, key) | The same string on another endpoint or in staging is a different universe |
| Retention | Server keeps keys at least 24h, matched to the client's maximum retry horizon | A retry landing after expiry executes as new - the guarantee is a lease |
| Stored value | The key plus the final result (status and body) of the first execution | A retry must replay the original outcome, including a stored failure, not re-execute |
| Same key, different payload | Reject with 422 | The key claims 'same operation'; a changed payload breaks the claim |
| In-flight duplicate | Second arrival while the first still runs: wait-and-replay, or 409 with a retry hint | Executing concurrently defeats the entire mechanism |

Two operational habits complete the design: log the key with every request so support can trace an operation across its attempts, and have clients audit 'distinct keys per operation' - the healthy value is exactly one, and any excess is a double-charge looking for a place to happen.

A provider's 429 response carries 'Retry-After: Fri, 27 Nov 2026 12:02:00 GMT' - an HTTP-date, not a number of seconds. Our client does int(retry_after) inside a try, and on failure treats the wait as 0 and retries immediately, which keeps the limit saturated. The response was received at 12:00:00 GMT the same day. Compute the wait the header actually requested:

arguments.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
header = "Fri, 27 Nov 2026 12:02:00 GMT"
retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(header)
now = datetime(2026, 11, 27, 12, 0, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
wait = int((retry_at - now).total_seconds())
print("Retry-After header:", header)
print("int(header) raises ValueError -> buggy client waits 0 s")
print("actual requested wait (seconds):", wait)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
Retry-After header: Fri, 27 Nov 2026 12:02:00 GMT
int(header) raises ValueError -> buggy client waits 0 s
actual requested wait (seconds): 120

The header asked for 120 seconds, and your client waited 0. Retry-After has two legal forms - a number of seconds, or an HTTP-date - and this provider used the date form. int('Fri, 27 Nov 2026...') raises ValueError, your error handler silently converts the parse failure into 'no wait requested', and the client retries instantly, re-saturating the limit it was just told to back away from. Parse failures on a backoff signal must fail toward waiting, never toward retrying: if the header cannot be understood, a conservative default (60 seconds, say) is the only safe fallback. The robust implementation tries delta-seconds first, then parses an HTTP-date and subtracts the response's Date header (or local receipt time), and clamps the result to something sane. This bug class - a parser that handles the common form of a header and silently degrades on the other legal form - recurs with dates, charsets, and encodings across every protocol. When a client is reported as 'ignoring' a server's instructions, check whether it ever actually read them; half the time the instruction arrived in a dialect the parser quietly dropped.

A worker retries a failing API call with exponential backoff: base 2 seconds, doubling, no cap, up to 13 attempts. The on-call noticed the job 'goes quiet for hours' near the end of its retry story. Print the schedule and total the damage:

arguments.code:
waits = [2 ** i for i in range(1, 9)]
print("waits for attempts 1-8 (s):", waits)
print("elapsed before attempt 9 (s):", sum(waits))
print("the wait before attempt 14 (s):", 2 ** 13)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
waits for attempts 1-8 (s): [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]
elapsed before attempt 9 (s): 510
the wait before attempt 14 (s): 8192

Uncapped doubling turns a retry policy into a disappearance: the waits run 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 seconds, so the job has already spent 510 seconds - eight and a half minutes - before its ninth attempt, and by attempt 14 a single wait is 8192 seconds, about 136 minutes of silence, as the calculator confirms. Two distinct harms follow. Operationally, a job that waits two hours between attempts looks dead: dashboards flatline, alerts for 'no progress' fire, and someone restarts it - often duplicating the work. Mathematically, the total elapsed time of an uncapped doubling schedule is dominated by the last wait, so 'a few more retries' quietly means 'tomorrow'. Every production backoff needs a ceiling (30-300 seconds is typical) after which the schedule becomes 'retry at the cap': waits like 2, 4, 8, 16, 30, 30, 30 keep pressure off the server while keeping the job visibly alive. Pair the cap with a total retry budget - maximum attempts or maximum elapsed time - after which the job fails loudly to a dead-letter queue. Backoff answers 'how long between tries'; the cap and budget answer 'when do we stop', and a policy missing either answer is unfinished.

A flash-sale incident: 200 client instances all received 429 with Retry-After: 60 at the same moment, all retried at exactly t+60 - and instantly got 429 again, in a loop that kept the API saturated for an hour. The server's limit is 50 requests/second. Model the retry instant, with and without jitter:

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content: The retry was perfectly synchronized, which made it a second outage scheduled by the first. Two hundred clients obeying the same Retry-After to the second produce 200 arrivals in one second against a 50/second limit - so three quarters of them are throttled again, receive the same instruction, and re-fire together a minute later: a self-sustaining oscillation that no amount of server capacity short of 4x headroom can absorb. Retry-After aligns clients; jitter is what disperses them. Spreading the same 200 retries across a 60-second window (each client waits 60 s plus a random offset) caps arrivals at 4 per second - comfortably under the limit, and the fleet drains instead of stampeding. The standard recipe is 'full jitter': sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)), and when a server sends Retry-After, treat it as the floor of the window, not the instant: wait Retry-After plus a random fraction of it. Any retry policy deployed to more than one machine needs randomness as a correctness property, not a nicety - synchronized clients are a distributed denial-of-service you inflict on yourself, politely, on schedule.

A nightly sync aborts on its first 429 and pages the on-call: 'job failed, API error'. The 429's headers were X-RateLimit-Limit: 1000, X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0, X-RateLimit-Reset: 1893456600, received at epoch 1893456000. The job had completed 80% of its pages before stopping. Read the headers and prescribe the behavior:

arguments.code:
headers = {"X-RateLimit-Limit": "1000", "X-RateLimit-Remaining": "0", "X-RateLimit-Reset": "1893456600"}
now = 1893456000
print("budget remaining:", headers["X-RateLimit-Remaining"], "of", headers["X-RateLimit-Limit"])
print("seconds until the budget resets:", int(headers["X-RateLimit-Reset"]) - now)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
budget remaining: 0 of 1000
seconds until the budget resets: 600

The API did not fail - it announced a ten-minute pause, and the job converted it into a page-out and a lost night. The headers say the budget of 1000 is exhausted (0 remaining) and resets in exactly 600 seconds. A 429 is a scheduling signal, not an error state: the correct response for a batch sync is to checkpoint, sleep until the reset (or the Retry-After, when present), and resume where it stopped - the 80% already fetched is banked work, and aborting throws away the schedule, not just the wait. Two design fixes follow. First, treat the rate-limit headers as telemetry during the whole run: when remaining drops toward zero, the client should throttle itself proactively and finish the window gracefully instead of face-planting into the wall at full speed. Second, reserve paging for conditions a human can act on; 'the API asked us to wait 600 seconds and we are waiting' is a log line, not an incident. Jobs that cry wolf on 429 train on-call teams to ignore the pager - which is how a real failure eventually gets slept through.

A client sends a steady 10 requests/second at an API governed by a token bucket: capacity 100 tokens, refill 5/second, one token per request. The client reasons 'the limit is 100, and I never burst more than 10 at once, so I am fine'. Simulate the bucket second by second and find when it first throttles:

arguments.code:
capacity = 100
refill = 5
send_rate = 10
bucket = capacity
first_throttle = None
for second in range(1, 61):
    bucket = min(capacity, bucket + refill)
    allowed = min(send_rate, bucket)
    bucket -= allowed
    if allowed < send_rate and first_throttle is None:
        first_throttle = second
print("bucket capacity:", capacity, "| refill/s:", refill, "| client rate/s:", send_rate)
print("first second in which requests are throttled:", first_throttle)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
bucket capacity: 100 | refill/s: 5 | client rate/s: 10
first second in which requests are throttled: 20

The client's mental model confuses the bucket's size with a rate. The bucket holds 100 tokens, but it refills at only 5 per second, so any sustained rate above 5/second spends the reserve: each second the client nets -5 tokens (10 out, 5 in), and the simulation shows the bucket hitting empty at the end of second 19 - the first throttled requests arrive in second 20, and from then on half the client's requests are rejected, every second, indefinitely. Burst capacity is a shock absorber for short spikes (a 100-request burst is fine, once), not a throughput entitlement; the sustainable rate of a token bucket is exactly its refill rate. The calculator confirms the other side of the coin: a fully drained bucket needs 100 / 5 = 20 quiet seconds to refill completely. Clients should read the pair (capacity, refill) as 'you may burst to capacity, but you live at refill' - pace steady traffic at or below the refill rate, save the bucket for genuine bursts, and when the API publishes only a per-minute number, treat short-window behavior as unknown and probe gently rather than assuming a bottomless burst.

An API log audit: six requests in a window - five returned 400 (malformed payload, a bug in our request builder) and one returned 200. Our retry policy retries every failed request 3 extra times regardless of status. The API quota counts every call. Audit the spend:

arguments.code:
log = [("req-1", 400), ("req-2", 400), ("req-3", 400), ("req-4", 200), ("req-5", 400), ("req-6", 400)]
attempts_per_failure = 4
bad = [r for r in log if r[1] == 400]
print("requests that could never succeed unchanged:", len(bad))
print("API calls the retry policy spent on them:", len(bad) * attempts_per_failure)
print("calls under a no-retry-on-4xx policy:", len(bad))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
requests that could never succeed unchanged: 5
API calls the retry policy spent on them: 20
calls under a no-retry-on-4xx policy: 5

Fifteen of the twenty calls spent on bad requests bought literally nothing. A 400 certifies that the request itself is malformed; resending the identical bytes three more times produces three more identical 400s, deterministically. The policy spent 20 calls on 5 hopeless requests where a status-aware policy spends 5 - and quota spent on guaranteed failures is quota unavailable for real work, which is how a request-builder bug escalates into a rate-limit incident: the retries quadruple the bad traffic, the 429s start, and now even the good requests fail. Retry policy must be status-aware at its core: 429 and 5xx are candidates (with backoff, and Retry-After honored); the rest of 4xx - 400, 401, 403, 404, 422 - are verdicts on the request or the credentials, and the only correct responses are to fix the request, fix the credentials, or stop. There is also a diagnostic cost: retry noise buries the original failure. One clean 400 in a log points at the builder bug in seconds; twenty of them look like an API problem and send the team hunting in the wrong building.

Forty separate tenant apps run behind one corporate NAT, so the provider sees a single source IP. The provider rate-limits per IP: 1000 requests/minute. Every few days, all forty tenants start getting 429s at the same time for about twenty minutes, though each tenant's own usage is modest and unchanged. One tenant runs a heavy reporting job 'a few times a week'. Explain the correlation, and what to ask the provider.

The forty tenants are not hitting forty limits - they are sharing one. Because the provider buckets by source IP and NAT collapses all forty apps into a single public address, the 1000 requests/minute is a communal budget, and one tenant's reporting job can spend it on behalf of everyone. The evidence fits perfectly: simultaneous 429s across unrelated tenants (their only shared resource is the egress IP), modest individual usage (each tenant is innocent in isolation), and a duration that matches a batch job's runtime. No tenant can fix this by behaving better; the well-behaved thirty-nine are throttled by the fortieth's burst. What to ask the provider, in order: (1) Can limits be keyed by API key or account instead of IP - most providers offer this, and it restores per-tenant fairness instantly. (2) If not, can they raise the per-IP ceiling for a known multi-tenant egress, or allowlist the NAT address with a higher tier? On your side, the mitigations are a shared egress proxy that queues and fairly schedules tenant traffic (turning an invisible commons into a managed one), per-tenant client-side quotas that sum to less than the shared limit, and moving the reporting job to its own egress IP. The debugging lesson generalizes: when failures correlate across systems that share nothing obvious, list what they do share - an IP, a DNS resolver, a cloud region, a single API key - because the limiter is almost always counting the shared thing.

Our runbook documents the retry policy as base 2 seconds, doubling. A client library's actual retry intervals, measured from its logs across one incident, were 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 seconds. The shape is right; something else is off. Compare against the documented schedule:

arguments.code:
documented_base = 2
expected = [documented_base * 2 ** i for i in range(5)]
observed = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]
print("documented schedule (base 2):", expected)
print("observed intervals:          ", observed)
print("observed equals base-1 schedule:", observed == [1 * 2 ** i for i in range(5)])

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
documented schedule (base 2): [2, 4, 8, 16, 32]
observed intervals:           [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]
observed equals base-1 schedule: True

The deployed client is running base 1, not the documented base 2 - every interval is exactly half the documented value, with the doubling intact. The observed sequence 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 is a perfect base-1 exponential, so this is not jitter or measurement noise; it is a different configuration value. Somewhere between the runbook and the runtime, the base was set to 1: an environment variable that never got applied in this deployment, a config file shadowed by a default, or a second client library with its own policy handling these calls. The practical impact is a fleet retrying twice as aggressively as designed - during an outage, that doubles the retry pressure at every step of the backoff, which is precisely when the policy exists to protect the recovering server. The debugging method is the keeper here: when behavior looks 'roughly like the policy', do not eyeball it - extract the actual intervals from logs and compare them term-by-term against the documented schedule. Configuration drift announces itself in exact arithmetic like this; a factor-of-two discrepancy across every term is a fingerprint, not a coincidence. Then fix the drift and add a startup log line that prints the effective policy, so the next drift is visible before the incident.

Load math review: an API client sets a 30-second timeout and retries each user request up to 6 total attempts. In a 5-minute window with 40 user requests during a partial outage (every attempt runs to the full timeout because the server is overloaded, not down), what does the client do to the server?

arguments.code:
user_requests = 40
max_attempts = 6
timeout_s = 30
total_calls = user_requests * max_attempts
print("user requests in the window:", user_requests)
print("worst-case API calls generated:", total_calls)
print("load amplification factor:", total_calls // user_requests)
print("server-worker seconds consumed:", total_calls * timeout_s)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
user requests in the window: 40
worst-case API calls generated: 240
load amplification factor: 6
server-worker seconds consumed: 7200

Forty user requests become up to 240 API calls, and because the server is overloaded rather than down, each of those calls holds a server worker for the full 30 seconds before the client gives up - 7,200 worker-seconds of demand generated by forty users. This is retry amplification, and it is why overloaded systems fall over completely instead of degrading: the client's remedy multiplies the disease sixfold, the extra load lengthens queues, longer queues cause more timeouts, and more timeouts trigger more retries. A timeout, crucially, does not mean the server stopped working on your request - in an overload it usually means the request is still queued or still running, so the retry is a second helping of work piled on the first. Defenses, in combination: far fewer attempts for expensive calls (2-3, not 6); a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing dependency entirely for a cooldown; retry budgets that cap retries as a fraction of total requests (say 10%), so a fleet cannot out-retry its own traffic; and server-side load shedding, where the server rejects fast with 503 + Retry-After instead of queueing work it cannot do - a fast rejection costs the server almost nothing and tells the client the truth. Retries are a loan taken against the server's spare capacity; in an outage there is none.

Give me a retry decision matrix we can pin above the on-call desk: for each situation - the HTTP status or failure kind, split by whether the request is a safe read or a state-changing write - should we retry, and if so, how?

Pin this up. The two questions that decide everything are 'could this request have taken effect?' and 'could sending it again change the answer?'

| Situation | Read (GET) | Write without idempotency key | Write with idempotency key |
|---|---|---|---|
| 429 | Retry after Retry-After | Retry after Retry-After | Retry after Retry-After |
| 503 | Retry, backoff + jitter | Retry, backoff + jitter | Retry, backoff + jitter |
| 500 / 502 | Retry, backoff + jitter, capped | Retry cautiously, capped | Retry, backoff + jitter |
| 504 / timeout | Retry | Do NOT blind-retry - reconcile first (query by your reference) | Retry - the key makes it safe |
| Connection refused | Retry, backoff | Retry - request provably never arrived | Retry |
| 400 / 422 | Never - fix the request | Never - fix the request | Never - fix the request |
| 401 | Only after refreshing credentials | Only after refreshing credentials | Only after refreshing credentials |
| 403 / 404 / 405 / 409 / 410 | Never (409: reconcile state first) | Never (409: reconcile state first) | Never (409: reconcile state first) |

Universal settings whatever the cell says: exponential backoff with a cap (e.g. 30-120 s), full jitter, a maximum attempt count and a total time budget, and every retry logged with its attempt number. The matrix's hardest row is the timeout on an unkeyed write - the honest answer is that the outcome is unknown, and 'unknown' is resolved by looking, not by resending.

After an API update, our integration reads user_name from the user payload and stores None for every user. The payloads look fine in the provider's explorer. A current payload is: {"username": "ada", "user_id": 7, "email": "ada@example.com"}. Our client reads the fields ['user_name', 'user_id']. Diff the two contracts:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
client reads 'user_name' -> present in payload: False | value: None
client reads 'user_id' -> present in payload: True | value: 7
fields the payload actually carries: ['email', 'user_id', 'username']

The provider renamed user_name to username, and your client has been reading a key that no longer exists. Because the code uses a tolerant .get(), the missing key becomes None instead of an exception, so every user syncs with a null name and no alarm fires anywhere - the payload 'looks fine' because it is fine; it is your field name that is a version behind. Field renames are the most common schema-drift break and the quietest, precisely because tolerant readers convert them into null data rather than errors. The defenses are contractual, not hopeful: read the provider's changelog at every version bump and diff the field sets (old keys versus new keys is a two-line check, as above); make required fields required in your parser, so a rename raises on the first record instead of rotting a million rows; and keep one captured real payload per endpoint as a contract test that fails when the shape moves. When a column of data goes uniformly null after a provider update, do not debug your storage - print the payload's actual key set and compare it with the keys your code asks for. The answer is usually staring at you in the diff.

An account-sync broke in a peculiar way: accounts exist, but lookups by id miss and reports show ids like 123 where the provider's dashboard shows 00123. The provider changed account_id from a JSON number to a string in their latest version, specifically to preserve leading zeros. Our client still coerces the value to int 'for consistency' before storing. Trace the value:

arguments.code:
provider_value = "00123"
coerced = int(provider_value)
print("provider sends account_id:", repr(provider_value))
print("after the client's int() coercion:", coerced)
print("written back to the API as:", repr(str(coerced)))
directory = {"00123": "Ada Lovelace"}
print("lookup by coerced id finds the account:", str(coerced) in directory)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
provider sends account_id: '00123'
after the client's int() coercion: 123
written back to the API as: '123'
lookup by coerced id finds the account: False

The leading zeros were information, and the int() coercion destroyed them. The provider moved account_id to a string precisely because these ids are identifiers, not quantities - '00123' and '123' are different identifiers in their system, the way '007' is not the number seven. Your client's coercion parses '00123' to the integer 123, stores and writes back '123', and from then on every lookup by the true id misses and every write-back addresses a different (or nonexistent) account. The rule underneath is absolute: never coerce an identifier to a number. Ids are opaque strings that happen to sometimes look numeric; the moment you do arithmetic-shaped operations on them - int(), float(), sorting numerically, formatting - you have asserted they are quantities, and they will eventually punish the assertion with leading zeros, ids beyond integer range, or embedded check digits. Type changes in a schema (number to string is a classic) are the provider's way of telling you the value's nature changed; when a field's type moves, audit every place your code touches it for silent coercions, including your own database column types.

A user clears their nickname in our app - we send {"nickname": null, "city": "Orlando"} to the API, where null means 'clear this field' and omitting a field means 'leave it unchanged'. The nickname never clears. Our client library has a 'helpful' preprocessing step that strips None values from outgoing payloads before sending. Show what the server actually receives:

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content: The server never hears about the nickname, because your client's cleaning step deletes the instruction. In JSON APIs, null and absent are two different signals: a field set to null is an explicit value ('clear this'), while an absent field says nothing ('leave it as it is'). The strip-Nones helper treats them as the same - it assumes None always means 'not provided' - and so an intentional clear is silently rewritten into a no-op. The city updates fine, which makes the bug look field-specific and mysterious. The same conflation bites in the other direction on reads: patch.get('nickname', old_value) returns None when the key is present with null and old_value when it is absent, and code that lumps them together cannot implement 'clear' semantics at all. Rules: never blanket-strip nulls from payloads - strip only fields your own model marks unset, with an explicit sentinel distinct from None; and when an API documents PATCH semantics, mirror them exactly: send nulls you mean, omit fields you do not. A field that 'refuses to clear' is this bug until proven otherwise.

After an API release, our address import stores empty cities everywhere. The v1 payload had a nested object: {"customer": "cus_4", "address": {"city": "Orlando", "zip": "32801"}}. The v2 payload flattened it: {"customer": "cus_4", "address_city": "Orlando", "address_zip": "32801"}. Our reader still navigates payload['address']['city'] defensively with .get() chains. Inspect the new shape:

arguments.code:
new = {"customer": "cus_4", "address_city": "Orlando", "address_zip": "32801"}
print("client reads address.city ->", new.get("address", {}).get("city"))
print("keys carrying the address data now:", sorted(k for k in new if k.startswith("address")))
print("the city, at its new key:", new["address_city"])

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
client reads address.city -> None
keys carrying the address data now: ['address_city', 'address_zip']
the city, at its new key: Orlando

The data did not disappear - it moved from a nested object to flat keys, and your defensive .get() chain is converting the move into silent emptiness. payload['address'] no longer exists, so .get('address', {}) yields an empty dict, .get('city') on that yields None, and the import dutifully stores None for every city while reporting success. Flattening and nesting are both legitimate shapes, and providers move between them during refactors more often than version numbers suggest; the defensive-reading style that protects you from a crash is exactly what lets the corruption through quietly. The repair has two layers. Immediate: read the flat keys (address_city, address_zip), ideally through a version-aware adapter that maps both shapes into your internal model, so the next reshape is a one-file change. Structural: validate a sample of imported records against invariants ('city is non-empty for US addresses') and alert on violation - a 100%-null column after a deploy is a five-alarm signal that costs one assertion to catch. Whenever a whole field goes uniformly empty at a provider boundary, suspect shape before data.

An order sync started crashing with KeyError: 'refunding'. The provider's order statuses were paid, pending, failed - our dispatch dict has exactly those three keys. This week the provider introduced a new status, 'refunding', for orders mid-refund-refund. Observed statuses in today's feed: paid, pending, refunding, paid, failed, refunding. Replay the dispatch:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
paid -> dispatch dict has a branch: True
pending -> dispatch dict has a branch: True
refunding -> dispatch dict has a branch: False
paid -> dispatch dict has a branch: True
failed -> dispatch dict has a branch: True
refunding -> dispatch dict has a branch: False
distinct values the handler cannot process: ['refunding']

Your handler treated an open set as a closed one. Status enums on a provider's side are not constants of nature - they are a list the provider extends whenever their business grows a new state, and 'refunding' is a perfectly ordinary addition. A dispatch dict keyed on exactly the values known at integration time converts every such addition into a crash, and the crash arrives not at deploy time but whenever the first order enters the new state - which is why it surfaced mid-week with no change on your side. The robust posture for consuming enums: always write the default branch. Unknown statuses should be handled by a safe fallback (store the raw value, mark the order 'unknown - needs review', alert once), never by exception and never by silently mapping to the nearest known value ('refunding' is not 'paid' and not 'failed', and pretending otherwise corrupts money state). Also version your assumption: keep the provider's current enum list in your contract tests by replaying a captured feed, so the day a new value ships, a test names it before production does. Providers will keep inventing states; your handler's job is to degrade, not detonate.

Receipts are wrong after the provider's v2 migration: a $42.00 charge prints as $4200.00. In v1, the field total was a float in dollars: 42.00. In v2, total is an integer in cents: 4200. Our formatting code was not changed - it prints '$%.2f' % total. Demonstrate, and give the boundary rule:

arguments.code:
v1_total = 42.00
v2_total = 4200
print("v1 value through the display code: $%.2f" % v1_total)
print("v2 value through the display code: $%.2f" % v2_total)
print("v2 value converted at the boundary: $%.2f" % (v2_total / 100))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
v1 value through the display code: $42.00
v2 value through the display code: $4200.00
v2 value converted at the boundary: $42.00

The number is right and the unit changed underneath it: v2's 4200 means cents, and your display code still reads it as dollars, inflating every amount exactly 100x. Unit changes are the most dangerous schema drift because nothing about the value looks wrong - 4200 is a plausible dollar figure, the JSON type even stayed numeric, and no parser complains. (The reverse migration, cents to dollars, is sneakier still: amounts shrink 100x and can hide inside rounding tolerances for weeks.) Providers change money representations for good reasons - integer cents eliminate float rounding - but the change is a breaking contract change and belongs in a version bump, which is your cue to audit. The boundary rule: convert units at the integration edge, the moment data enters your system, into your canonical unit, with the provider version explicitly known; never let two unit conventions coexist inside your code, and never let a money value travel without its unit being obvious from the field name or the type (an int named total_cents is self-documenting; a bare total is a trap). When totals jump by exactly 100x (or 1000x, for milliseconds-versus-seconds style units), do not debug arithmetic - diff the contract.

A user sync fails for SOME users since Tuesday, all with 'unknown field' errors from our own strict deserializer, which rejects any payload key outside its known set {id, email, plan}. The provider began including a new field, signup_source, populated only for users who signed up via the web. Three current payloads: user 1 {id, email, plan}, user 2 {id, email, plan, signup_source}, user 3 {id, email, plan}. Run the deserializer's rule:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
user 1 -> accepted: True | unknown fields: []
user 2 -> accepted: False | unknown fields: ['signup_source']
user 3 -> accepted: True | unknown fields: []

Your deserializer is rejecting reality for containing more than your model of it. The provider added signup_source - an additive, backward-compatible change by every normal convention - but a deny-unknown-fields parser converts any addition into a failure, and because the field is populated for only some users (web signups), the failure is partial: users 1 and 3 sail through while user 2 hard-fails, which is why the sync looks flaky instead of versioned. Partial failures that correlate with a subpopulation are a schema-drift fingerprint. The consumer-side rule is Postel's: be liberal in what you accept. Unknown fields should be ignored (or better, logged once and preserved if you re-emit the object), because providers will add fields constantly and almost never announce the harmless ones. Strictness has its place - on data you produce, and in security-sensitive parsing - but on inbound integration payloads it is a self-inflicted breaking-change amplifier. Fix the deserializer to ignore unknowns, then go further: add the new field to your model deliberately if it is useful, and treat 'sync fails for a correlated subset' as a prompt to diff one failing payload against one passing payload, key by key. The diff is always the diagnosis.

A PHP-backed API represents item lists in a way that keeps biting our Python client. A non-empty list sometimes arrives as a JSON object with numeric string keys - {"items": {"0": "a", "1": "b"}} - and an empty list arrives as {"items": {}}. Our client iterates the value expecting a list of items. Show what iteration actually yields in each form:

arguments.code:
import json
list_form = json.loads('{"items": ["a", "b"]}')
object_form = json.loads('{"items": {"0": "a", "1": "b"}}')
empty_form = json.loads('{"items": {}}')
print("list form:   iterating gives", list(list_form["items"]))
print("object form: iterating gives", list(object_form["items"]))
print("empty form:  type is", type(empty_form["items"]).__name__, "| length", len(empty_form["items"]))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
list form:   iterating gives ['a', 'b']
object form: iterating gives ['0', '1']
empty form:  type is dict | length 0

The client is iterating dictionary keys and calling them items. When the collection arrives as a JSON object - which this encoder produces whenever the underlying array's keys are not a clean 0..n sequence, and for empty collections - Python iteration over it yields the keys '0', '1' as strings, so downstream code processes the strings '0' and '1' instead of the values 'a' and 'b', and the empty case arrives as a dict rather than a list at all. This is a representation leak from the producer's language: PHP arrays are ordered maps, and JSON encoding of a map with sequential integer keys produces a list, while any gap, filtering, or string-keying produces an object - the same logical collection, two wire shapes, chosen by accident of content. The consumer's fix is a normalization shim at the boundary: if the value is a dict, convert it to a list of its values ordered by integer key (an empty dict becomes an empty list); if it is already a list, pass it through. Normalize once, at the edge, into the shape your domain expects, and never let the producer's encoding habits leak into business logic. When a collection field misbehaves only for some records - empty ones, filtered ones - suspect shape instability, not data.

Dates in a partner feed silently broke: our parser expects %Y-%m-%d and the partner used to send '2026-11-05'. They now send '1793836800' - epoch seconds as a string. The parser throws, a broad except swallows it, and the date lands as null in our warehouse. Untangle the two formats:

The partner changed the representation, not the dates: '1793836800' is epoch seconds for exactly 2026-11-05 UTC - the same day the old format would have carried. Your pipeline's real bug is the broad except that converts a parse failure into a null and carries on; a format change at a feed boundary should be a loud, run-stopping event, and instead it became a slow leak of null dates into the warehouse, discovered by a human reading a report. Date and time fields are the most format-unstable part of any API contract - ISO strings, epoch seconds, epoch milliseconds, and locale formats all circulate, and providers migrate between them. Defenses: parse defensively but fail loudly (accept the documented formats, reject anything else with an alert, never default to null); validate feed-level invariants after each load ('zero null dates' is a one-line check that would have caught this on day one); and pin the expected format in a contract test with a captured sample. Note the epoch value is also unit-ambiguous - had it been milliseconds, the same string would mean 1970 - which is why epoch fields must be documented with their unit and why a value like 1793836800 (10 digits, seconds-scale) versus 1793836800000 (13 digits, milliseconds) should be sanity-checked by magnitude.

A partner's form-encoded endpoint sends booleans as strings: active=true or active=false. Our Python client stores the raw value and later checks 'if record.active:' to decide whether an account is enabled. Deactivated accounts keep working. Demonstrate the trap with the actual values:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
wire value: 'true' | Python truthiness of the string: True
wire value: 'false' | Python truthiness of the string: True
conclusion: the string 'false' is truthy - every account tests as active

The string 'false' is a non-empty string, and every non-empty string is truthy in Python - so an account the partner deactivated sails through your check as active. The bug is a type that changed at the boundary without anyone noticing: JSON endpoints deliver real booleans, but this form-encoded partner delivers the text 'true'/'false', and code that stores the raw value and leans on truthiness silently promotes the text to a boolean role it cannot play. Nothing crashes; the logic is just wrong for exactly the accounts that matter most - the disabled ones - which makes this a security-shaped bug, not a cosmetic one. The fix is explicit parsing at the boundary: map the wire strings to real booleans with a strict function (accept exactly 'true' and 'false', raise on anything else), and store only the parsed boolean. The general principle: truthiness is not parsing. Any value arriving from a wire is text until you convert it, and conversions for booleans, numbers, and dates should be deliberate, validated, and located in one adapter layer - because 'the API changed how it encodes a field' is a when, not an if, and the adapter is where you want that discovery to happen.

Our test records: id 1 has tax_id T-1, id 2 has none, id 3 has tax_id T-3, id 4 has none. Sort out who fails and why the pattern looks random:
